To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the SSRs are more frequent in the lower plants, such as algae and mosses.
SSRs are more abundant in lower plant species than in higher plants, and that the dimer motifs are predominant in lower plant species and the trimer in higher plant species.

the SSR marker distribution patterns in the EST databases of the eleven species are in agreement with the evolutionary trends observed for plant lineages and the SSR marker transferability between species is in general higher in the lower plant groups than in the higher plant groups.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification, characterization and comparative analysis of SSRs from EST databases of eleven plant species.
the identification of SSR markers in the EST databases for eleven model plants and with the comparative analysis of SSR occurrence in the ESTs of these model plants.
the identification of SSR markers for all plant lineages.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SSRs are more frequent in plant genomes and that the SSR frequency decreases with the increasing plant genome size.
the SSR markers are more frequent and more abundant in the lower plant species, and the higher plant species are richer in SSR markers with longer repeat units.
the SSR markers are highly conserved in the higher plants, but not in the green algae and moss, as well as the lower plant species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SSR markers are more abundant in the lower plant groups and the higher plant groups have more SSR markers in the trimer motif.
the EST-SSR marker survey is useful for comparative studies among plant species, and that it could also be used to predict the occurrence of EST-SSRs in a given plant group.
the EST-SSR marker discovery is a useful tool for comparative plant genomics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SSR marker discovery in EST sequences is a reliable and fast method for plant comparative studies.
the SSRs are not evenly distributed in the plant genome.
the EST-SSR marker survey can be used as a tool to study evolutionary patterns and to predict transferability of molecular marker in plant species.
